items_missed: Never asked 'how are you today?' or ran any warm-up — straight from the greeting into the date confirmation.

Availability for the move date never checked or confirmed. She confirmed September 26th is the customer's date but never told her Einstein has it open. This customer ended the call saying she is shopping around; she leaves with no idea whether we can even do her Saturday.

No agenda statement. 'Is this a good time to talk about your move?' is a permission ask with no roadmap and no timeframe — the customer never learned what the next eleven minutes would contain, which matters because the call ran almost eleven minutes on a two-and-a-half-hour minimum job.
Additional rooms never probed — no balcony, no patio, no storage closet at the apartment.

Packing needs never asked. She asked about box counts but never asked whether the customer wanted help packing, and never offered the service — on a customer who volunteered 'I have not been able to get a hold of the rest of the furniture' and is clearly under time pressure to be out.
No 'pricing is super simple' opener — she went straight into 'because here at Einstein, we charge an hourly rate.'
Packing service pricing never given.

No Worries Damage Coverage never mentioned. 'Insurance' appears once, as a word inside the inclusions list — no $2,000, no repair/replace/reimburse, no brand name, no 60-cents-per-pound contrast. This is a customer moving a standing freezer, a mini fridge and small appliances into storage; damage coverage is directly relevant and she heard nothing.
Meet Your Mover never mentioned.
On-Time Guarantee never mentioned.

Clock start never explained — nothing about the clock starting on-site when the contract opens, which matters on this job because the crew is running two addresses across San Antonio and the customer has no idea whether she is paying for that drive.

No sense-check anywhere in the pricing or clock block. She ran the rate, the inclusions, the trip fee, the no-hidden-fees list, the minimum and the proration in one continuous stretch and then went straight into the estimate without once asking if it landed. The customer's total contribution across it was 'Mm-hmm.'
Truck count never stated — she said 'two movers' and never mentioned a truck at all.

Drive time never explained. The pickup is 78257 and the storage unit is 78230 — a real cross-town run in San Antonio — and she never told the customer whether that drive is on the clock. She disclosed a $70 travel fee but never connected it to the drive between locations.
Traffic never mentioned as a variable, on a Saturday cross-town move.
No equivalents or plain-language anchors used anywhere.

The 50-to-100-foot breezeway walk was captured and then never factored. The customer gave a genuinely useful access answer — 'it's about a fifty to a hundred foot walk from like what the closer entrance' — and the estimate that followed went to the absolute floor with no mention of it. Either the walk does not matter, in which case do not ask, or it does, in which case say so.
Save Your Ass entirely absent — 0/10. No prep-saves-you-money line, no consolidation examples, no carload tip, no close.

Zero booking attempt. The customer said 'I'm shopping around so I'll make it back to you guys when I'm, once I've gone through my other options' and the entire response was 'Okay, no worries.' No offer to hold September 26th, no urgency, no specific follow-up date, no ask of any kind.
No deposit required was never mentioned — the highest-cost miss on this call. 'I'm shopping around' is precisely the objection that no-deposit answers, because it makes holding the date free.

BOLDED-details framing absent, and the 'reply with any corrections' verification ask absent. She said 'just reply to that email' — but to book, not to verify — after collecting a unit number, a storage address, an inventory list and an access description entirely by ear with no read-back.

No 'any other questions before I let you go?' at the close. She asked the concerns question before pricing, which is good placement, but nothing after the number — so the estimate landed and the call ended.
Hours never given — 'give us a call' with no hours and no direct line.
Customer's name never used once across 10.9 minutes. She used 'ma'am' repeatedly instead.
top_strength: Jeline's discovery is the second-strongest in this batch and her specialty-item probing is genuinely systematic — she runs a real checklist rather than asking one open question and hoping. In sequence: 'you don't have any workout equipment a safe or a washer or dryer,' 'How about a TV that is more than sixty inches?', 'Do you have anything available like our pieces or anti collections?' That is the heavy/fragile/high-value sweep, asked in full, on a job that turned out to have none of it — which is exactly when the discipline counts, because it is the calls where nothing turns up that reps skip. She also handled the storage side better than anyone would need to: she nailed down that it is a 10x10 on the first floor and then asked the question that actually changes the labor — 'Is this an outdoor storage unit or a climate' — and got the answer that it is drive-up, which is what let her quote at the floor. And she chased access properly: 'at the current apartment, can we just park in front of your, in front of your unit?' produced the whole breezeway problem, fifty to a hundred feet, entrance at either end of the building. Her best single stretch is the estimate construction, which is the model for what Amanda's accuracy work is trying to produce. She gave the benchmark first, then adjusted off it with named reasons, and adjusted downward: 'normally for a one bedroom apartment. We finish the move-in three and a half to four and a half hours but in your case we're only moving few pieces of furniture here and boxes from the first floor apartment going to a drive up storage unit. So, I will only estimate the move to be on the minimum of two and a half to three hours just to give you a range.' Benchmark, three specific job facts, revised range, and then the protection: 'of course, this is only my estimate, if the move will only take about the minimum hours, then you will only be charged for the minimum charge of $585.' That is the anti-padding behavior, stated out loud, with the reasoning audible to the customer. The other real strength is the FAQ answer. The customer asked a confused, half-formed question about whether she had to follow the truck and how the movers get through the storage gate, and Jeline gave a complete answer that also protected the company: 'you don't really need to follow with the truck... You can definitely give us the code for the storage unit, but of course, we want you to be present as well at the storage unit in case you have any instructions, and of course ma'am the payment will be collected after we completed the move. So, we really need you to be at the storage unit.' Three things resolved in one answer, including the payment logistics the customer had not thought to ask about.
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix: Jeline did nine minutes of excellent discovery, built the most defensible estimate in the batch, and then closed nothing. The customer said 'I'm shopping around so I'll make it back to you guys' and got 'Okay, no worries.' That is the entire close. Everything that could have held this customer was available and unused — the date was still open, there is no deposit, and her number was likely to be competitive precisely because she quoted the floor instead of padding it. The line: 'Totally fair, and you should compare. One thing that might help while you do — we don't take a deposit and there's no card on file, so I can hold Saturday the 26th for you right now at no cost. If you find something better you just reply and let me know and I'll release it. That way shopping around doesn't cost you the date.' That single paragraph delivers the booking attempt and the no-deposit differentiator, both of which are currently zero. Second priority: the differentiator block is missing entirely. No Worries, Meet Your Mover and On-Time Guarantee are all absent, which means the only thing this customer can compare us on is $206 an hour plus a $70 travel fee — and against a cheap local competitor that is a comparison we lose. She is moving a standing freezer and a mini fridge into a storage unit; $2,000 of included damage coverage is a concrete reason to pay more, and it was never said. Install the same fixed thirty-second block after the rate every call. Third, the sense-check. Her entire pricing-and-clock explanation ran as one uninterrupted block and the customer's only contribution was 'Mm-hmm.' Adding 'does that all make sense so far?' after the rate is worth a rubric point, but more importantly it is the difference between a customer who has heard the number and a customer who has understood it — and the one who understood it is the one who calls back. No estimate-accuracy flag on this call; it runs the right direction. She quoted 2.5 to 3 hours against her own stated 3.5-to-4.5 benchmark and named the three facts that justified going low. Worth using alongside Garrison Cobe's call from the same week as a positive example in the bottom-4 calibration sessions — both reps shaded down off a benchmark using access facts, which is the exact behavior the rock is chasing. One caveat to raise with her, though: she captured a fifty-to-a-hundred-foot breezeway walk with no direct parking and then quoted the absolute minimum without ever mentioning it. Quoting low is right when the facts support it, but a long carry is a fact that pushes the other way and it disappeared from her reasoning. If this one books and runs over 2.5 hours, the carry is why — worth pulling the actual. Last, efficiency: 10.9 minutes to quote a two-and-a-half-hour minimum job is too long, and the transcript shows why. She lost the inventory thread mid-call and had to restart it ('Mm-hmm what are the other furniture that you'd like a, I'), and there are several places where she and the customer talked over each other. Tightening discovery would free up the two minutes the differentiators and the close actually need.
phone_presence_notes: Polite and patient with a customer who was genuinely hard to follow, and one real warmth moment — 'okay, understood. Thank you for sharing that with me' — but the call is otherwise transactional and heavily padded with 'Mm-hmm' and 'Uh-huh' rather than acknowledgment, the customer's name is never used once across eleven minutes, and there are several stretches where Jeline loses the thread and has to re-ask ('Okay, but are you there?', 'Oh, sorry just been second'), which reads as processing rather than listening.
audio_review_reason: The clarity-and-pace and efficiency bullets were both deducted on transcript evidence that is genuinely ambiguous. The transcript shows repeated overlap, interjections landing out of sequence, and several abandoned sentences from Jeline ('Okay, are there an?', 'And that's gonna.', 'I'll drive out.'), plus a stretch where she asks 'Okay, but are you there?' mid-conversation. From text alone there is no way to separate three very different causes: a bad line, a rep processing slowly while typing, or a transcription artifact from two people with different accents talking over each other. The coaching is completely different in each case, so this one needs audio before any feedback is given.
